intro.html: Six of these words are verbs for what puzzles do to us: they perplex, baffle, bewilder, confound, befuddle and flummox. The other four name the puzzles and the fixes we find ourselves in. Notice the difference: you are in a quandary, you face a dilemma, and you try to solve a conundrum or an enigma.

Verbs (to confuse): perplex, baffle, bewilder, confound, befuddle, flummox. Nouns: conundrum (the hard puzzle itself), quandary (your state of not knowing what to do), dilemma (a hard choice between two options) and enigma (a mystery, often a person).

words.def: to confuse and trouble someone with something hard to understand
words.ex: The strange thumping in the attic {perplexed} the whole family.
words.ctx: The math problem {perplexed} even the teacher at first; she stared at it for a full minute before she spotted the trick hidden in the second line.
words.etym: From Latin perplexus, “tangled, confused”: per (thoroughly) + plexus (woven, braided).

mn.text: Ivy finds a big X painted on the sidewalk, with no note and no arrow. It {perplexes} her all week.

scene.alt: A puzzled girl scratches her head over a big X painted on the sidewalk.

words.def: to be too hard for someone to understand or solve
words.ex: The locked-room mystery {baffled} every detective in the city.
words.ctx: The magician’s last trick {baffled} the audience; though they watched his hands closely, no one could explain how the rabbit ended up in the front row.

mn.cue: BAF-FLE: the cookies FLEW out of a locked jar?
mn.text: The cookie jar is still locked, but every cookie is gone! The mystery {baffles} Dev and Lila. (The cat isn’t talking.)

labels.text: BAFFLE: HOW did they get out?

scene.alt: Two puzzled teens stare at an empty, locked cookie jar while a cat winks in the corner.

words.def: to confuse completely, often with too many things at once
words.ex: The huge airport, with its hundred gates and blinking signs, {bewildered} Granny Mae.
words.ctx: The new phone’s menus {bewildered} Dad: every button opened three more choices, and soon he had no idea how to get back to the start.
words.etym: From be- (thoroughly) + an old verb wilder, “to lead astray,” as if into a wilderness.

mn.text: Sami steps off the trail, and the jungle closes in around him: vines everywhere, paths in every direction. He is {bewildered}.

scene.alt: A dizzy boy with a backpack stands lost in the jungle as a monkey and a parrot look on.

words.def: to confuse and surprise; also, to prove a prediction wrong
words.ex: The tiny team {confounded} the experts by winning the whole tournament.
words.ctx: The results {confounded} the scientists; the plants kept in the dark had somehow grown taller than the ones in the sun, the opposite of what everyone expected.
words.etym: From Latin confundere, “to pour together, to mix up”: con (together) + fundere (to pour).
words.note: Confound has two senses: to confuse (the riddle confounded us) and to prove wrong (the results confounded the experts).

mn.cue: con-FOUND: the experts FOUND they were wrong
mn.text: Everyone said the little team couldn’t win, but they did. The experts found they were wrong, and the surprise win {confounds} them.

scene.alt: Two small children hold up a trophy while two shocked experts who predicted they would lose stare in disbelief.

words.def: to muddle someone’s thinking; to confuse
words.ex: The long list of rules {befuddled} the new players.
words.ctx: The riddle seemed simple, but its twist {befuddled} Kai; he said the answer was “Tuesday,” then “a candle,” then gave up and asked for a hint.
words.etym: From be- (thoroughly) + fuddle, an old word meaning “to confuse.”

mn.text: Dev’s new video game has a hundred rules. His thoughts turn into a puddle of muddle, and his player keeps walking into walls. The game {befuddles} him.

scene.alt: A teen on the sofa stares at his game controller, confused by what the television is showing.

words.def: to confuse someone so completely that they don’t know what to do
words.ex: The self-checkout machine {flummoxed} Dad, who kept scanning the same banana.
words.ctx: The tangle of pipes under the sink completely {flummoxed} the new plumber; he stared at it, scratched his head and finally called his boss for help.
words.etym: An English dialect word of the 1800s whose origin is unknown.

mn.cue: FLUM-OX: the OX is totally STUMPED
mn.text: The ox stares and stares at the gate latch, nudges it, then stares some more. He has no idea what to do: it {flummoxes} him.

scene.alt: A confused ox stares at a closed farm gate, with no idea how to open it.

words.def: a confusing and difficult problem; also, a riddle
words.ex: How to fit six bikes into a tiny garage was a real {conundrum}.
words.ctx: The town faced a {conundrum}: the old bridge was too weak for buses, yet tearing it down would cut the village off from the school for a whole year.
words.etym: Of unknown origin; it first appears in English in the 1500s.

mn.cue: CONE + DRUM: how do they fit?
mn.text: Jamal has to fit a giant drum, a traffic cone and a tuba into one tiny car. It’s a real {conundrum}!

scene.alt: A puzzled man wonders how to fit a giant drum and a traffic cone into a tiny car.

words.def: a state of not knowing what to do
words.ex: Invited to two parties on the same night, Rosa was in a {quandary}.
words.ctx: Lost on the trail as the sun went down, the hikers were in a {quandary}: should they keep walking in the dark or camp where they were and wait for morning?
words.etym: Of uncertain origin; it first appears in English in the 1500s.
words.note: A quandary is the uncertain state you are in; a conundrum is the puzzle itself.

mn.cue: QUAN-DARY: WANDERING, not knowing what to do
mn.text: Pip has one dollar to spend, and he wanders up and down the toy store, back and forth, unable to choose. He is in a {quandary}.

scene.alt: A worried boy with a dollar paces back and forth in a toy store, unable to choose.

words.def: a hard choice between two options, often both unpleasant
words.ex: Lila faced a {dilemma}: her best friend’s party and her cousin’s recital were both on Saturday at noon.
words.ctx: The coach faced a {dilemma}; if she pitched her star player today, he would be too tired for the final, but if she rested him, the team might lose today’s game.
words.etym: From Greek dilemma, “a double proposition”: di (two) + lemma (a premise, something taken for granted).
words.note: A dilemma is a choice between two options, often both bad, not just any problem.

mn.text: Kai must eat one of two sour lemons; whichever he picks, he’ll pucker. Two choices, both sour: that is a {dilemma}.

scene.alt: A worried boy shrugs between two sour lemons, unhappy with either choice.

words.def: a person or thing that is mysterious and hard to understand
words.ex: The new neighbor was an {enigma}: no one ever saw him come or go, yet his garden was always perfect.
words.ctx: To the scientists, the strange signal remained an {enigma}; it arrived every night at three o’clock, from no known star, and no one could explain it.
words.etym: From Greek ainigma, “a riddle,” from ainissesthai, “to speak in riddles.”

mn.cue: a masked MYSTERY: who is it?
mn.text: Every evening a stranger in a mask leaves a single flower on the park bench and slips away. No one knows who it is: the stranger is an {enigma}.

scene.alt: At night, a masked stranger in a cape leaves a flower on a park bench while a teen watches, puzzled.

after.cap: The puzzle, the fix you are in, the choice and the mystery.

after.html: A dilemma is a hard choice between two options (di- means two), often both unpleasant; don’t use it for just any problem. The six verbs are close cousins, but confound has a second sense, to prove a prediction wrong, and bewilder often suggests being lost among too many things at once.

opts.s: The magician’s last trick {baffled} the audience; no one could explain how the rabbit ended up in the front row.
opts.why: The blank needs a verb: the trick was too hard to understand. It baffled them.

choices: choosing between two summer camps that fall on the same week
items.why: A dilemma is a hard choice between two options. The others are problems, but they offer no choice between two paths.

items.q: “I’m in a ______; I just can’t decide what to do.” Which word fits best?
items.why: You are in a quandary: it is the state of not knowing what to do. A conundrum is the puzzle itself.

items.q: True or false: confound can mean to prove a prediction wrong.
items.why: True. When the underdogs win, they confound the experts who said they would lose.
Di- means two, as in dioxide: a dilemma offers two choices.

items.q: Type the noun for a person or thing that is mysterious and hard to understand.
items.why: An enigma is a mystery, from Greek ainigma, a riddle.
